newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian Tiger economies hit bump, but still a force.
newsitem.headline: Asian Tiger economies hit bump, but still a force.

text.p: Labour convulsions in South Korea and limp export growth among Asia's other Tiger economies have set off alarm bells in government offices and boardrooms from Seoul to Kuala Lumpur.
Western sceptics of the "Asian miracle" are asking whether the export juggernauts have lost their competitive edge.
But economists across Asia say the Tigers -- namely Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore -- are not an endangered species.
They say they are still a competitive force in world markets and the export slump is mainly due to cyclical factors.

Nevertheless, South Korea -- as well as countries such as Thailand -- must address important issues such as labour reform to boost efficiency and fight off growing competition from emerging economies with lower labour costs.
South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Tiger cub Malaysia have been hit by a global downturn in prices for their leading exports, notably semiconductors.
In South Korea, where striking workers have thrust the issue of labour reform on to the agenda in the past three weeks, total exports rose only 3.8 percent last year to $129.83 billion.
"Korea is not losing its teeth," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investments & Securities Co Ltd.
He said falling export growth and corporate profitability were the result of a normal cyclical downturn.
Economists said Thailand's export slump was more troubling and the country was losing its advantage of cheap labour to Indonesia, China and Vietnam.
They said structural woes had emerged from a failure to pump enough money into medium technology industries to substitute for traditional, labour-intensive businesses such as textiles.
Export growth in 1996 was negative at minus 0.1 percent against 24 percent growth in 1995.
Malaysia, which once relied on rubber, tin and palm oil for exports, is one of the world's largest makers of semiconductors and in its ninth year of more than eight percent growth.
It has shifted quickly from labour-intensive to capital and technology-intensive industries. Economists estimate Malaysia's exports will increase by 10 to 15 percent this year.
"The country continues to grow fast, maybe a bit too fast," said Liew Yin Sze, regional economist with J.M. Sassoon & Co in Singapore.
A big hurdle for the Tigers, which is symptomatic of their success, has been growing incomes, leading to higher wages.
Taiwan remains an export powerhouse, but rising incomes have eroded its low-cost manufacturing prowess -- especially with the emergence of neighbouring China's vast labour market.
Taiwan's exports grew just 3.9 percent in 1996 to US$116 billion, while imports slipped 2.2 percent to US$101 billion. State economists predict eight percent growth for both in 1997.
Taiwan has shifted to more profitable, high value-added manufacturing, chiefly in computers and electronics.
Daniel Harwood, regional director at HG Asia in Seoul, said South Korea was waking up to the need for wrenching change.
"Korea is on the cusp of having to make some pretty radical moves such as restructuring to bring down costs to make the place more efficient," he said.
"My feeling is increasingly that they really have woken up and realised what the situation is."

The government rammed a controversial bill through parliament late last year to free up the labour market, arguing it needed to trim corporate costs and boost competitiveness. Wages have grown 15 percent annually over the past decade.
The move triggered more than three weeks of strikes and street clashes between workers and police.

South Korea became the 29th member of the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development in December. Since applying to join the Paris-based club of rich nations in March 1995, Seoul has accelerated the opening of its financial markets to foreign investors and pledged further reforms.

In Singapore, which now has per capita income of around US$24,000, inflated land, raw material and wage prices have driven up costs for companies and forced most low-technology manufacturing industries to move elsewhere.
But economists say it is far too early to strip the tiny island republic of its status as a Tiger economy.
In Hong Kong, economic growth has slowed gradually over the past 10 years reflecting a structural shift in the territory's economy from manufacturing to services.
Hong Kong now relies on re-exports, goods shipped through Hong Kong into China for processing, and then re-exported out through Hong Kong.
"Hong Kong's production costs are not important now, what counts are China's production costs," said Eddie Wong at HG Asia in Hong Kong.
"Chinese inflation is coming down and wage growth will come down this year, so no, I don't think Hong Kong is losing its competitiveness," Wong said.
